beats.narration_text: Namaste. I'm Riya Kapadnis, and this is my final project pitch for INFO seventy-three seventy-five. People ask whether an AI can write SQL. The better question is whether its SQL is right on your data, and how you would know.

'any good' corrected to 'right on my data'

beats.narration_text: Three terms. Text to SQL: a model turns a plain English question into a database query. A gold set: questions with answers I checked by hand. And execution match: judging a query by the rows it returns, not its wording.

the right SQL, checked by hand
judge SQL by its output table

beats.narration_text: Here is the project. Ground Truth SQL will be an evaluation harness. You give it your database and a set of questions, and it tells you which questions the model gets wrong, and why.

beats.narration_text: When it's done, it will be a public GitHub repository with three parts: about fifty checked questions, a runner that asks Claude each one, and a scorecard listing every failure and its cause. Today, only a first slice exists.

beats.narration_text: Why care? A query can run, look right, and still be wrong. In my first test, a query I wrote by hand to copy a common join mistake put US revenue at four thousand six hundred sixty seven dollars. The real number is five hundred twenty three. Nine times too high, and no error.

shot.visual_intent: Two bars side by side on a plinth: a short one '523' (checked) and a tall one '4,667' (join mistake) that grows about nine times taller; caption 'real run · 2026-10-09'.
shot.motion_claim: Two bars side by side on a plinth: a short one '523' (checked) and a tall one '4,667' (join mistake) that grows about nine times taller; caption 'real run · 2026-10-09'.

beats.narration_text: I looked at two alternatives. BIRD is a benchmark of over twelve thousand questions, but on its own ninety five databases, not yours. Vanna writes SQL for your own database, but I didn't find a way in it to test that SQL against checked answers. Mine does that: your schema, checked answers, and a reason for every failure.

shot.visual_intent: Left: a tall shelf of many pages labelled 'BIRD'. Middle: a workstation labelled 'Vanna'. Right: the project's crate with a check, labelled 'your schema'.

beats.narration_text: The check is simple. Run the checked query and the model's query on the same read only database, and compare the rows. On my first eight questions, comparing the SQL text rejected all three correct rewrites. Comparing rows judged all nine test queries the way I did.

shot.visual_intent: Two trays side by side, 'gold' and 'model'; matching row blocks drop into each; a scan line passes and a check lands; a counter reads '9/9'.

beats.narration_text: It also caught me. My first gold answer asked about revenue in twenty twenty three, but this data stops in twenty thirteen. The checked answer was empty, so a broken query matched it. Now the runner rejects any empty gold answer.

beats.narration_text: Who opens it? A hiring manager or engineer screening AI engineers. In the first minute, they'll read the scorecard, replay the saved results with one command and no key, and open one failure beside its checked answer.

beats.narration_text: What should it prove? That I evaluate models instead of trusting them: a prompt contract that allows one read only select, verification by running the SQL, failures sorted by cause, and later a repair loop I'll measure. The evidence will be dated logs anyone can re-run.

beats.narration_text: What could sink it? I write both the questions and the answers, so the test could be too easy, or wrong, like twenty twenty three. So a classmate will check a sample of my answers, unclear questions will be marked unclear, and each question will run three times.

beats.narration_text: Why this project? It's a mix. SQL, Python, and building language model features into a BI product are skills I use in my AI engineer co-op, but that code is private, so my public evidence is this course's work. Evaluation sets, failure analysis, and measured repair loops are new to me, and that's what I want to learn.

shot.visual_intent: Two shelves: left 'have' with a stack of pages and a check; right 'learning' with an empty slot a block slides into.

beats.narration_text: So, what exists today is eight questions, one comparator, and one bug I caught in my own answers. Everything else is still to build. Models that write SQL are easy to find. Knowing when to trust them is the project.
